standard_text: Understand that a function assigns to each x-value (independent variable) exactly one y-value (dependent variable), and that the graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs (x, y); determine whether a relation (set of ordered pairs, table, mapping, or graph) is a function.

progression.narrative: Standard 8.AF.3 asks students to know that a function assigns each input exactly one output and to test any relation, whether ordered pairs, a table, a mapping, or a graph, against that rule. The on-grade skills move from naming independent and dependent variables, to stating the definition, to scanning lists and tables for a repeated input with different outputs, to the vertical line test on graphs. The error that dominates is judging by outputs: students disqualify a relation because a y-value repeats, when only a repeated x-value with different y-values breaks the rule. Students who stall here usually cannot read ordered pairs or graphs reliably, so intervention drops back to grade 5 coordinate grid work and grade 4 input-output rule tables. The grade 7 bridge skills, deciding whether a table shows a constant rate of change and interpreting a point (x, y) on a real-world graph, rebuild the table scanning and graph reading the function tests depend on.

steps.rationale: Before you can test a relation you must know which number is the input (independent variable) and which is the output (dependent variable). This settles the vocabulary the whole standard leans on and where the input/output confusion first appears.
State the definition precisely -- each input has exactly one output -- and reject the reversed version (each output has one input). The definition is the tool every later determination applies.

Apply the definition to a set of ordered pairs: scan for a repeated x-value paired with different y-values. This is the core grade-level determination and where the 'repeated output' misconception is corrected.
Run the same input-uniqueness test on a table or mapping. A new representation with the identical logic forces the criterion to transfer beyond ordered-pair notation.

Because the graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs (x, y), testing a graph is the vertical line test -- does any single x sit under two points. This extends the criterion to the visual representation named in the standard.

The above-grade synthesis: decide whether a real-world relation is a function, justify with the definition, and critique a classmate who judged by a repeated output. Proves students own the asymmetric rule, not just a procedure.

skills.name: Plot and name points on the coordinate grid using ordered pairs

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot a point from an ordered pair (x, y) in the first quadrant, and name the ordered pair for a plotted point: across first, then up.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot the point (3, 5), how far do you go across, and how far up?

skills.i_do_script: An ordered pair is walking directions on the grid: start at 0, go across first, then up. Watch (3, 5): I put my finger at the corner, walk 3 spaces across, then 5 spaces up, and mark the point. The first number is always the across number, the x. The second is always the up number, the y. If I flip them and walk 5 across and 3 up, I land on a different spot, so the order matters every time.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the order and goes up first or swaps the coordinates
canonical_error.example: Plots (3, 5) by going 5 across and 3 up, landing on (5, 3)
canonical_error.why: The student does not hold the fixed order: across first (x), then up (y). Same digits in the other order name a different point, and the grid shows the two spots are not the same.

skills.item_template: A first-quadrant coordinate grid with whole-number points. Student plots a point from an ordered pair or names the ordered pair for a marked point. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: To plot (3, 5), how many spaces do you go across?
To plot (3, 5), how many spaces do you go up?
A point is 4 across and 1 up. Write its ordered pair.
A point is 0 across and 6 up. Write its ordered pair.
Which point is farther to the right: (2, 8) or (7, 1)?
Which point is higher up: (2, 8) or (7, 1)?
Do (4, 6) and (6, 4) land on the same spot? Answer yes or no.
sample_items.answer: No

sample_items.stem: A point sits on the x-axis at 5 across. Write its ordered pair.

redirect_script.stop: Which way do you walk first, across or up?
redirect_script.prompt: Start at 0. The first number walks you across, the second walks you up. Say it as you move your finger: across 3, up 5.
redirect_script.praise: You walked across first and then up, so you landed exactly where the pair says.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers written (x, y) that name one point on the grid: across first, then up.
The horizontal number line on the grid; the first number counts along it.
The vertical number line on the grid; the second number counts along it.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 5 coordinate graphing with a labeled first-quadrant grid: finger at 0, walk across, then walk up.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a first-quadrant grid. Plot (3, 5) by walking a finger 3 across and 5 up. Then plot (5, 3) the same way.
Same digits in both pairs. Why are the two points in different places?
The first number is always the across number and the second is always the up number. (3, 5) walks 3 across and 5 up, and (5, 3) walks 5 across and 3 up, so they land on different spots.
If a student walks up first, stop them at 0 and say the rule while they move: across first, then up.
Your turn: plot (2, 6), then write the ordered pair for a point 6 across and 2 up.

skills.name: Follow a rule to complete an input-output table

prerequisite_skill.description: Given a rule such as add 3 or multiply by 2, find the output for each input in a table.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: The rule is add 3. The input is 5. What is the output?

skills.i_do_script: Picture a machine with an IN slot and an OUT slot. The rule is what the machine does to every number that goes in. Watch the rule add 3: I drop in 5, the machine adds 3, and 8 comes out. I drop in 9 and 12 comes out. Every input gets the same rule, and each input gives back exactly one answer. In the table, the input column is what goes in and the output column is what comes out, row by row.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies the rule inconsistently or fills the output column with a pattern instead of using the rule on each input
canonical_error.example: For the rule multiply by 2 with inputs 3, 5, 10, writes outputs 6, 8, 10 by adding 2 each row instead of doubling each input
canonical_error.why: The student extends a pattern down the output column instead of applying the rule to each input. The rule acts on the input in the same row, not on the output above it.

skills.item_template: A rule such as add 3, subtract 4, or multiply by 2, and one or more whole-number inputs. Student finds each output. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Rule: add 3. Input: 5. What is the output?
Rule: add 3. Input: 9. What is the output?
Rule: multiply by 2. Input: 7. What is the output?
Rule: subtract 4. Input: 10. What is the output?
Rule: multiply by 5. Input: 6. What is the output?
Rule: add 10. Input: 25. What is the output?
Rule: multiply by 2. The output is 16. What was the input?
Rule: subtract 4. Input: 4. What is the output?

redirect_script.stop: What does the rule do to the number that goes in?
redirect_script.prompt: Take one row at a time. Say the rule out loud, drop the input into it, and write what comes out: input 5, add 3, output 8.
redirect_script.praise: You ran the rule on each input, one row at a time. That is exactly how the machine works.

vocabulary.definition: The number that goes into the machine or table.
The number the rule gives back for an input.
What is done to every input to get its output, like add 3 or multiply by 2.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 number patterns with a drawn function machine: rule in the middle, number in, number out.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a machine with an IN slot, the rule multiply by 2 written in the middle, and an OUT slot. Next to it, draw a table with inputs 3, 5, 10 and an empty output column.
Drop 3 into the machine. What comes out? Now drop in 5.
3 doubles to 6, 5 doubles to 10, and 10 doubles to 20. Each row is its own trip through the machine, and each input comes back with exactly one output.
If a student writes 6, 8, 10 by adding 2 down the column, point at the machine: the rule works on the input in that row, not on the answer above it.
Your turn: rule add 3, inputs 2, 6, 11. Fill in the outputs.

skills.name: Determine from a table whether the rate of change is constant or varying

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare how much y changes for each step in x down a table and decide whether the rate of change is constant or varying.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 3, 5, 7, 9. Is the rate of change constant or varying?

skills.i_do_script: A rate of change compares how much y moves each time x steps forward. Watch the table x = 1, 2, 3, 4 with y = 3, 5, 7, 9: each time x goes up 1, y goes up 2, then 2, then 2. The change is the same every step, so the rate of change is constant and the table describes a linear relationship. Now x = 1, 2, 3, 4 with y = 2, 4, 8, 16: y jumps by 2, then 4, then 8. The jumps are different, so the rate of change is varying. I always write the jump between every pair of rows before I decide.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges by the y-values themselves instead of by the changes between rows
canonical_error.example: Calls x = 1, 2, 3, 4 with y = 3, 5, 7, 9 varying because 3, 5, 7, 9 are different numbers
canonical_error.why: The student looks at whether the outputs repeat instead of whether the jumps between them repeat. A constant rate means the change from row to row is the same, not that the y-values are the same.

skills.item_template: A table of x and y values with equal x steps (occasionally steps of 2). Student finds the change in y per step and decides constant or varying. MC or short response.

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 3, 5, 7, 9. Is the rate of change constant or varying?
sample_items.answer: Constant. y goes up 2 every time x goes up 1.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Varying baits students who see that the y-values differ; the jumps are all +2.

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 2, 4, 8, 16. Is the rate of change constant or varying?
sample_items.answer: Varying. y jumps by 2, then 4, then 8.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Constant baits students who see doubling as a repeated action; the jumps are different sizes.

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 10, 8, 6, 4. Is the rate of change constant or varying?
sample_items.answer: Constant. y goes down 2 every step.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Varying baits students who think a decrease cannot be constant; the change is -2 every step.

sample_items.stem: In the table x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 4, 7, 10, how much does y change each time x goes up 1?
sample_items.answer: It goes up 3.

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 0, 2, 4, 6 and y = 0, 6, 12, 18. How much does y change for each 1 unit of x?
sample_items.answer: 3. y goes up 6 for every 2 units of x, which is 3 per unit.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 6 baits students who ignore that x steps by 2 in this table.

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 1, 4, 9, 16. Is the rate of change constant or varying?
sample_items.answer: Varying. y jumps by 3, then 5, then 7.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Constant baits students who spot the squaring pattern and call any pattern constant.

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 5, 5, 5, 5. Is the rate of change constant or varying?
sample_items.answer: Constant. y changes by 0 every step, and 0 every time is still the same change.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Varying baits students who think no movement means no rate; a change of 0 each step is constant.

sample_items.stem: Which kind of table describes a linear relationship: one with a constant rate of change or one with a varying rate of change?
sample_items.answer: One with a constant rate of change.

redirect_script.stop: Are you comparing the y-values or the jumps between them?
redirect_script.prompt: Write the change between every pair of rows in the margin: +2, +2, +2. Constant means the jumps match, not that the y-values match.
redirect_script.praise: You wrote out every jump before deciding. That is the whole test.

vocabulary.definition: How much y changes for each 1 unit that x changes.
The same change in y for every equal step in x; the mark of a linear relationship.
Jumps in y that are different sizes for equal steps in x.

worked_example_script.text: Build two cube-tower sequences: towers of 3, 5, 7, 9 cubes, and towers of 2, 4, 8, 16 cubes. Line each set up left to right.
How many cubes do you add to get from each tower to the next in the first set? In the second set?

The first set grows by 2 cubes every time, the same jump, so its rate of change is constant. The second grows by 2, then 4, then 8, different jumps, so its rate is varying. The table x = 1, 2, 3, 4 with y = 3, 5, 7, 9 is just the first set of towers written down.
If a student says the first set is varying because the towers are different heights, point at the added cubes: is the number you ADD the same each time?
Your turn: x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 10, 13, 16, 19. Write the jumps and decide constant or varying.

practice_problems.stem: In the table x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 4, 6, 8, how much does y go up each step?
If y changes by the same amount for every equal step in x, is the rate of change constant or varying?
practice_problems.answer: Constant

practice_problems.stem: x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 7, 10, 13, 16. Constant or varying? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Constant. The jumps are +3, +3, +3.

practice_problems.stem: x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 1, 2, 4, 8. Constant or varying? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Varying. The jumps are +1, +2, +4.

practice_problems.stem: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and y = 20, 15, 10, 5. Constant or varying? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: Constant. y changes by -5 every step.

practice_problems.stem: x = 0, 2, 4 and y = 0, 10, 20. What is the change in y for each 1 unit of x?
practice_problems.answer: 5. y rises 10 for every 2 units of x.

practice_problems.stem: Write a table of four rows with x = 1, 2, 3, 4 whose rate of change is constant at 4 per unit, starting at y = 3.
Kira decided whether a table has a constant rate of change. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Kira wrote: 'Varying, because 6, 9, 12, and 15 are all different numbers.'
practice_problems.answer: Kira compared the y-values instead of the jumps between them. The jumps are +3, +3, +3, the same every step, so the rate of change is constant.

activities.title: Tower Jumps
materials: Linking cubes or square tiles
Whiteboards
activities.instructions:
1. Build the towers 3, 5, 7, 9 from cubes and line them up.
2. Count the cubes ADDED between neighboring towers and write each jump on the board: +2, +2, +2.
3. Build the towers 2, 4, 8, 16 and write those jumps: +2, +4, +8.
4. Label each set constant or varying and copy each set into a table of x (tower number) and y (cubes).
5. Say each time: the test is the jumps, not the heights.

activities.title: Constant or Varying?
materials: Card set of 10 small x-y tables, half constant and half varying
activities.instructions:
1. For each table card, write the jump between every pair of rows in the margin.
2. Sort the cards into Constant and Varying.
3. To place a card, read your jumps out loud; the group must agree they are right.
4. Debrief: one card has y = 5, 5, 5, 5. Why is it constant?

strategy_links.why: Cube towers make the jump between rows a countable object before the rate-of-change rule is named.
Judging by y-values instead of jumps is a stable error; finding and fixing it in shown work confronts it directly.
Thinking aloud while writing +2, +2, +2 in the margin models the scan students should run on every table.

questioning_prompts: What is the jump in y between these two rows?
Are you comparing the y-values or the changes between them?
The x column steps by 2 here. How does that change the rate per unit?
Can a rate of change be constant if y is going down?
Which of these tables could describe a linear relationship, and how do the jumps tell you?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls a table varying because the y-values are different numbers.
misconception_redirects.say: The y-values are supposed to move. Write the jump between every pair of rows: is the JUMP the same each time?
misconception_redirects.praise: You tested the jumps, not the values. That is the real test.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student ignores the x column and computes jumps across unequal x steps as if they were per unit.
misconception_redirects.say: Check the x column first. If x steps by 2, the jump in y covers 2 units, so cut it in half to get the rate per unit.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the change in y to the step in x before naming the rate.

quick_checks.prompt: x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 8, 11, 14. Constant or varying?
quick_checks.look_for: Constant, with the jumps +3, +3 written or stated. Varying diagnoses judging by values.

quick_checks.prompt: x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 2, 4, 7. Constant or varying?
quick_checks.look_for: Varying, because the jumps are +2 then +3.

worked_solution.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 3, 5, 7, 9. Is the rate of change constant or varying?

steps.annotation: Compare each pair of neighboring rows.
x steps by 1 each row, so each jump is per unit.
Write every jump before deciding.

steps.math: all jumps equal 2, so the rate is constant
steps.annotation: Same change for every equal step in x means constant.

faded_example.stem: A table shows x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and y = 2, 6, 10, 14. Is the rate of change constant or varying?

steps.annotation: Compare the first pair of rows.
x steps by 1, so this jump is per unit.
Find the last jump.
Compare the jumps and decide constant or varying.

sentence_starters: The jumps in y are ___, so the rate of change is ___.
The rate is constant because y changes by ___ for every ___ in x.

skills.name: Interpret a point (x, y) on the graph of a real-world relationship

prerequisite_skill.description: Read a point from a real-world graph and state what its coordinates mean, with the x-axis quantity first.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A graph shows cost in dollars for pounds of apples. What does the point (3, 12) mean?

skills.i_do_script: Every point on a real-world graph is one fact, and the axes tell you how to read it. Watch a graph with pounds of apples on the x-axis and cost in dollars on the y-axis. The point (3, 12) sits 3 across and 12 up, so it says 3 pounds cost 12 dollars. I always read the axis labels first, then say the fact with the x-axis quantity first: 3 pounds, 12 dollars. The point (1, 4) on the same graph says 1 pound costs 4 dollars, the cost for a single unit.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads the point backwards, attaching the x-coordinate to the y-axis quantity
canonical_error.example: Says (3, 12) on a pounds-vs-cost graph means 12 pounds cost 3 dollars
canonical_error.why: The student ignores which axis carries which quantity. The first coordinate always belongs to the x-axis label and the second to the y-axis label, so (3, 12) is 3 pounds and 12 dollars.

skills.item_template: A described real-world graph with labeled axes and one or more named points. Student states what a point means, or names the point that matches a described fact. Short response or MC.

sample_items.stem: A graph shows pounds of apples on the x-axis and cost in dollars on the y-axis. What does the point (3, 12) mean?
sample_items.answer: 3 pounds of apples cost 12 dollars.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The reversed reading, 12 pounds for 3 dollars, swaps the axes.

sample_items.stem: A graph shows hours on the x-axis and miles on the y-axis. What does the point (2, 90) mean?
sample_items.answer: In 2 hours, 90 miles were traveled.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 90 hours for 2 miles reverses the coordinates.

sample_items.stem: On a graph of hours worked (x) and dollars earned (y), which point shows earning 45 dollars in 5 hours: (5, 45) or (45, 5)?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (45, 5) puts the dollars on the hours axis.

sample_items.stem: A graph of gallons (x) and miles driven (y) passes through (1, 30). What does that point tell you?
sample_items.answer: 1 gallon takes the car 30 miles. It gives the miles for a single gallon.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 30 gallons for 1 mile reverses the axes.

sample_items.stem: A graph of minutes (x) and liters of water (y) passes through (0, 0). What does that point mean?
sample_items.answer: At 0 minutes, 0 liters have been dispensed; nothing has happened yet.

sample_items.stem: On a graph of tickets bought (x) and total cost in dollars (y), the point (4, 32) is marked. How much does each ticket cost?
sample_items.answer: 8 dollars, because 4 tickets cost 32 dollars and 32 divided by 4 is 8.

sample_items.stem: A graph shows days (x) and plant height in cm (y). Write the point that says the plant was 15 cm tall on day 6.
sample_items.distractor_logic: (15, 6) puts the height on the day axis.

sample_items.stem: Two points on a savings graph of weeks (x) and dollars saved (y) are (2, 30) and (5, 75). Which point shows more money saved?
sample_items.answer: (5, 75), because the second coordinate is the dollars saved.

redirect_script.stop: What does the x-axis measure on this graph? And the y-axis?
redirect_script.prompt: Read the axis labels first. Then say the fact with the x-axis quantity first: the first coordinate goes with the x-axis label, the second with the y-axis label.
redirect_script.praise: You matched each coordinate to its axis label before saying the fact. That is exactly how a point is read.

vocabulary.definition: The quantity an axis measures, like pounds on the x-axis or dollars on the y-axis.
One ordered pair (x, y): one fact pairing an x-axis amount with a y-axis amount.
The point (0, 0), where both quantities are zero.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a first-quadrant graph with pounds of apples on the x-axis and cost in dollars on the y-axis. Plot (3, 12) and (1, 4).
Before we touch the points: what does the x-axis measure? What does the y-axis measure?
The point (3, 12) sits over 3 on the pounds axis and level with 12 on the dollars axis, so it says 3 pounds cost 12 dollars. The point (1, 4) says 1 pound costs 4 dollars.
If a student says 12 pounds cost 3 dollars, trace straight down from the point to the x-axis: what number and what label do you hit?
Your turn: on the same graph, what would the point (2, 8) mean?

practice_problems.stem: On a graph, which axis does the first coordinate of a point belong to?
practice_problems.answer: The x-axis (the horizontal axis).

practice_problems.stem: A graph shows hours (x) and pay in dollars (y). What does (1, 9) mean?
practice_problems.answer: 1 hour of work pays 9 dollars.

practice_problems.stem: A graph shows minutes (x) and laps run (y). What does the point (12, 4) mean?
practice_problems.answer: In 12 minutes, 4 laps were run.

practice_problems.stem: On a graph of bags (x) and oranges (y), write the point that says 5 bags hold 40 oranges.
A savings graph of weeks (x) and dollars (y) passes through (0, 0) and (3, 45). What does each point mean?
practice_problems.answer: (0, 0): at week 0 nothing is saved yet. (3, 45): after 3 weeks, 45 dollars are saved.

practice_problems.stem: A graph of gallons (x) and miles (y) passes through (2, 56). How many miles per gallon is that?
practice_problems.answer: 28 miles per gallon, since 56 divided by 2 is 28.

practice_problems.stem: A point on a pounds (x) versus cost (y) graph is (4, 10). Write the point that would show the cost of 8 pounds at the same price per pound.
practice_problems.answer: (8, 20), since 4 pounds cost 10 dollars, so each pound is 2.50 and 8 pounds cost 20 dollars.

practice_problems.stem: Leo read a point on a graph of hours (x) and miles (y). Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Leo wrote: 'The car went 3 miles in 120 hours.'
practice_problems.answer: Leo swapped the axes. The first coordinate belongs to the x-axis, hours, and the second to the y-axis, miles. The point means the car went 120 miles in 3 hours.

activities.title: Say the Point
materials: Large first-quadrant grid (poster or whiteboard)
Sticky dots
Axis label cards (hours/dollars, pounds/cost, minutes/liters)
activities.instructions:
1. Pick an axis label card and tape the labels to the grid, x-axis quantity first.
2. Partner A places a sticky dot on any grid point and traces down to the x-axis and across to the y-axis.
3. Partner B says the fact out loud in a full sentence, x-axis quantity first: 3 hours earned 27 dollars.
4. Swap roles, then change the label card and repeat.
5. Finish by writing each spoken fact as an ordered pair (x, y).

activities.title: Point-Fact Match-Up
materials: Card deck: one card per point with its axis labels, one card per fact sentence
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each point card, such as (2, 90) on an hours-miles graph, to its fact sentence.
3. To claim a match, read the axis labels first, then the sentence.
4. Two decoy sentences read the point backwards; set them aside and explain the swap.

pairs.right: On day 6 the plant was 15 cm tall

strategy_links.why: Tracing from the point down to one axis and across to the other makes the coordinate-to-label pairing visible before any rule is stated.
The reversed reading is a precise, common error; finding and fixing a swapped sentence corrects it directly.
Saying each point as a full sentence with a partner forces the axis-first reading into language.

questioning_prompts: What does the x-axis measure? What does the y-axis measure?
Trace straight down from the point. What number and label do you hit?
Say the point as a sentence, x-axis quantity first.
What does the point (0, 0) mean in this story?
Which point on this graph shows the amount for a single unit?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student attaches the first coordinate to the y-axis quantity.
misconception_redirects.say: Read the labels before the numbers. Trace down to the x-axis: that label owns the first coordinate. Then trace across for the second.
misconception_redirects.praise: You let the axes assign the numbers. That reading is now trustworthy.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads the coordinates correctly but cannot say what the point means in the story.
misconception_redirects.say: Turn the pair into a sentence using the axis words: 3 on pounds, 12 on dollars, so 3 pounds cost 12 dollars.
misconception_redirects.praise: You turned the pair into a fact from the story. That is what the point is for.

quick_checks.look_for: 4 hours earned 36 dollars. '36 hours' diagnoses the axis swap.

quick_checks.prompt: Write the point that says 7 gallons drove 210 miles on a gallons (x) vs miles (y) graph.

The first coordinate always belongs to the x-axis label.
The second coordinate belongs to the y-axis label.
Say the fact with the x-axis quantity first.

The first coordinate goes with the x-axis.
Attach the second coordinate to its axis label.

skills.name: Identify the independent and dependent variables in a relation
skills.i_do_script: Picture each ordered pair as one run of a machine: you drop the FIRST number in the IN slot, and the machine hands the SECOND number back out. In (3, -5), you chose the 3 -- the -5 is what came back in response. The independent variable is the INPUT -- the x-value, the first number in each ordered pair, the quantity you choose or control. The dependent variable is the OUTPUT -- the y-value, the second number, the quantity that responds. Watch the set {(3, -5), (-2, 4), (7, 1)}: the independent variables (x-values) are 3, -2, and 7, the first number in each pair. The dependent variables (y-values) are -5, 4, and 1. Input first, output second, every time.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the roles -- names the y-value (output) as the independent variable
canonical_error.example: For (3, -5) calls -5 the independent variable instead of 3

skills.name: State the definition of a function: each input has exactly one output
skills.i_do_script: A function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output -- each x-value has exactly one y-value. Say it as a one-way promise: every input points to a single output. Watch the trap: the reverse, 'every OUTPUT has exactly one input,' is NOT the definition. A function is allowed to send different inputs to the same output; it just can't send one input to two different outputs. So the correct definitions are 'every x has exactly one y' and 'every independent variable has exactly one dependent variable.'

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the definition -- states that each output has exactly one input
canonical_error.example: Chooses 'every y-value has exactly one x-value' as the definition of a function
canonical_error.why: The rule is one-directional: each INPUT maps to exactly one output. A function may send different inputs to the same output, so the restriction lives on the inputs, not the outputs.

skills.name: Determine whether a set of ordered pairs is a function
skills.i_do_script: To decide if a set of ordered pairs is a function, I hunt for a REPEATED x-value that is paired with DIFFERENT y-values. If I find one, it is not a function; if every x-value is different (or a repeat has the same y), it is a function. Watch {(2, 5), (3, 7), (2, 9), (4, 5)}: x = 2 shows up twice, once with y = 5 and once with y = 9 -- two different outputs for one input, so this is NOT a function. Notice y = 5 also repeats (with x = 2 and x = 4), but repeated OUTPUTS are fine; only a repeated input with different outputs breaks it.

canonical_error.pattern: Disqualifies a relation because a y-value (output) repeats, instead of checking for a repeated x with different y
canonical_error.example: Calls {(2, 3), (4, 3), (6, 3)} 'not a function' because the output 3 repeats, when every input is different so it IS a function
canonical_error.why: The student applies the rule to outputs instead of inputs. Repeated outputs are allowed; only a repeated INPUT paired with two different outputs violates the definition.

skills.name: Determine whether a table or mapping represents a function
skills.i_do_script: Think of the table as a machine's logbook: each row records what went IN and what came OUT. A working machine is allowed to give the same answer to different inputs -- but it can NEVER give two different answers to the same input. So the only column that can break a function is the input column. A table or mapping is a function by the same test as ordered pairs: read the input (x) column and look for a repeated input tied to different outputs. Watch a table with x = 1, 2, 3, 5 and y = 4, 4, 4, 4: every x is different, so even though the outputs are all 4, each input has exactly one output -- it IS a function. Now a table with x = 2, 4, 2, 6 and y = 5, 7, 8, 9: x = 2 appears twice with 5 and 8, two outputs for one input, so it is NOT a function. In a mapping, a function has exactly one arrow leaving each input.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges the table by the OUTPUT column -- calls repeated y-values a non-function (or requires all outputs to differ)
canonical_error.example: Says a table with x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 5, 5, 8 is 'not a function' because two outputs are 5, when every input is different so it IS a function
canonical_error.why: The student scans the wrong column. A table is a function when each INPUT appears with one output; repeated outputs across different inputs are allowed.

skills.name: Determine whether a graph is a function using the vertical line test
skills.i_do_script: Because the graph of a function is the set of ordered pairs (x, y), testing a graph is just checking inputs visually: the VERTICAL line test. If any vertical line (a line straight up and down at a single x-value) touches the graph in more than one point, that x-value has two outputs, so it is NOT a function. Watch a straight slanted line like y = 2x: every vertical line crosses it exactly once, so it IS a function. A circle fails: a vertical line through the middle hits it at two points. Careful -- it is the VERTICAL line you slide across, not a horizontal one.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses a horizontal line test (or checks for repeated y-values) instead of the vertical line test
canonical_error.example: Calls a horizontal line y = 3, or an upward U-shaped parabola, 'not a function' because many x-values share the same y-value
canonical_error.why: The student tests outputs instead of inputs. The rule is about each input having one output, so the line you slide must be VERTICAL (one x at a time); repeated y-values do not matter.

skills.item_template: A graph described as plotted points or as a named curve. Student applies the vertical line test. MC / short response. (Figures are described in text so the item is render-safe.)

sample_items.stem: A graph consists of the plotted points (1, 2), (2, 4), (1, 5), and (3, 1). Does the graph represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. A vertical line at x = 1 passes through both (1, 2) and (1, 5), so x = 1 has two outputs.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Two points share x = 1 -> vertical line hits twice -> not a function.

sample_items.stem: A graph is a straight slanted line rising to the right (like the line y = 2x). Does it represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Every vertical line crosses the slanted line exactly once, so each x has one y.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Passes the vertical line test.

sample_items.stem: A graph is a circle. Does it represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. A vertical line through the middle of the circle crosses it at two points, so one x has two y-values.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Fails the vertical line test.

sample_items.stem: A graph is a single vertical line at x = 4. Does it represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. The input x = 4 is paired with every y-value on the line, so it has more than one output.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A vertical line is the extreme failure: one x, infinitely many y. Baits confusing 'vertical line test' with 'the graph is a vertical line.'

sample_items.stem: A graph is a U-shaped parabola opening upward (like y = x squared). Does it represent a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Every vertical line crosses the parabola exactly once, so each x has one y (even though outputs repeat on the two sides).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Baits the horizontal-line/repeated-output error; it passes the vertical line test.

skills.name: Justify whether a real-world relation is a function and critique reasoning
skills.i_do_script: In a real-world relation I first decide which quantity is the input (independent variable) and which is the output (dependent variable), then apply the same test: does any input have two different outputs? Watch the kayak table -- hours rented paired with cost, where cost stays at 20 after hour 4. A classmate says it is not a function because the cost 20 repeats. But hours is the INPUT and each hour appears once, so each input has one cost. The repeated OUTPUT does not matter -- it IS a function. I justify with the definition, and I check whether a critique is judging by the input or the output.

canonical_error.pattern: In a context, judges function-status by whether the OUTPUT values repeat rather than the inputs
canonical_error.example: Says the kayak cost table {(1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15), (4, 20), (5, 20), (6, 20)} is not a function because the cost 20 repeats, when each hour (input) is unique so it IS a function
canonical_error.why: The student picks the wrong quantity as the one that must be unique. Function-status depends on each INPUT having one output; repeated real-world outputs (same price, same height) are allowed.

skills.item_template: A real-world relation as a table or story, sometimes with a classmate's claim. Student decides, justifies, or critiques. Multi-part.

sample_items.stem: A machine dispenses water by seconds: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 8) [seconds, liters]. Is this a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Each number of seconds (input) gives exactly one amount of water, so it is a function.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Every input appears once -> function.

sample_items.stem: A store records (price, shirt color): $10 -> red, $10 -> blue, $15 -> green. Is 'price -> color' a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. The price $10 (input) is paired with two different colors (red and blue), so one input has two outputs.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Repeated input $10 with different outputs -> not a function.

sample_items.stem: A kayak rents by the hour; after hour 4 the price stays at $20. Table [hours, cost]: (1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15), (4, 20), (5, 20), (6, 20). A classmate says it is NOT a function because the cost 20 repeats. Is the classmate correct? Explain.
sample_items.answer: The classmate is incorrect. Hours is the input and each hour appears once, so each input has one cost -- it IS a function. The repeated output ($20) is allowed.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Critique targets the repeated-output error; unique inputs make it a function.

sample_items.stem: A girl records her height each birthday, ages 4 to 9 [age, height]: (4, 40), (5, 43), (6, 45), (7, 48), (8, 50), (9, 53). Is this relation a function? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Each age (input) has exactly one height, so it is a function.
sample_items.distractor_logic: All inputs (ages) unique -> function.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, deciding whether a set of ordered pairs is a function, the At-proficiency core where the repeated-output misconception lives. If they pass, move through S4 (tables and mappings) and S5 (graphs, vertical line test). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks whether they can scan a table and compare rows through constant versus varying rate of change, and B2 checks whether they can read a point (x, y) off a real-world graph, the two grade 7 skills the function tests lean on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (plotting and naming coordinate points, grade 5) and F2 (input-output rule tables, grade 4) locate the gap. S1 and S2 remain available to probe the standard's own vocabulary and definition, and S6 branches off as the above-grade synthesis.
